Hardware Security & Supply Chain

The Spy Beneath the Screen

When a genuine secure element confirms authenticity, but a rogue cellular implant sniffs recovery words directly from the display bus.

By Federico Rivi · [s551]

A genuine hardware wallet, purchased brand-new from an authorized reseller, can quietly pass every official software verification check while simultaneously delivering its owner's recovery seed straight into the hands of remote attackers.

That is the sobering reality documented in Federico Rivi's detailed investigation into compromised Ledger devices originating from Southeast Asian authorized reseller CryptoBilis. In affected units, attackers added an intercept circuit beneath the display screen. The device's Secure Element—the hardened microcontroller executing cryptographic routines—remained completely original and untouched. But when the unit generated recovery words and pushed pixels to the display, the hidden circuit captured the bus signals, assembled the words, and broadcast them over an embedded cellular eSIM.

As Rivi explained, the computer may be clean and the owner may have followed every precaution for storing the backup, but the copy is made earlier, inside the device. The core dilemma is the fundamental gap between cryptographic authenticity and physical integrity. As Ledger's Donjon security research group made clear in their documentation, the automated genuineness check confirms that the genuine chip remains intact; it does not detect foreign hardware spliced into peripheral traces. Customers who kept their seeds strictly on paper and operated entirely offline still watched their balances drained.

The reverberations across the industry have been swift. Competitor Trezor moved quickly to scale back its authorized reseller distribution channels, terminating contracts by January 2027 to narrow the attack surface of physical transit. Meanwhile, unverified reports of compromised retail stock in Germany led to temporary sales halts before retail inspections found no tampering, prompting researcher Kevin Loaec to walk back early alarms.

For affected owners, security guidance is uncompromising: importing old seed phrases into fresh hardware merely restores keys that may already be compromised. True safety requires new entropy generated on clean, trustworthy hardware, followed by a swift on-chain sweep of all assets.

Confidential Inference

Zero Providers Pass Every Gate

In the inaugural issue of Attested, Aljaz subjects trusted execution environments and enclave routers to rigorous verification.

By Aljaz · [s550]

Hardware isolation is steadily making its way into mainstream machine learning pipelines. In the debut edition of Attested, Aljaz charts the rapid expansion of confidential inference—from Brave Leo routing end-to-end encrypted chats through NEAR AI's Intel TDX enclaves, to hash-pinned DeepSeek model weights running on Tinfoil within 24 hours of release.

Yet Aljaz’s automated monitoring tools reveal a massive gulf between marketing assertions and verifiable end-to-end provenance. Of 97 independent verification checks conducted across 11 commercial inference providers, 55 successfully cleared hardware and Trusted Computing Base (TCB) hurdles. But exactly zero passed every rigorous policy gate when evaluating workload identity, source provenance, and request routing.

Before anyone gets too excited - the prompt still gets decrypted. The model has to read it. What you get is operator isolation: the hardware is supposed to keep infrastructure operators (NEAR and Brave included) from reading what the attested code inside the enclave is processing.

Aljaz cautions against overreaction, noting that the score reflects strict gate definitions rather than an absolute absence of security. Nevertheless, with academic vulnerabilities such as FABRICKED and STALEUS targeting AMD SEV-SNP without physical access, relying on unverified claims from intermediary routers remains a precarious gamble.

Protocol Progress

Payer Notes Land on BOLT12

Self-hosted Lightning payments gain structured communication and persistent records.

By Alex71btc⚡💜₿🚀 · [s4]

The Lightning Network has long suffered from a UX asymmetry: sending value was instant, but attaching human context required out-of-band coordination. With the release of BOLT12 Pay v0.3.15 on Umbrel and StartOS, incoming payer notes are now directly integrated into node activity.

The release allows senders using compatible wallets such as Phoenix to include emojis, multi-line notes, and formal invoice references, storing the resulting history persistently alongside offer memos. As developer Alex71btc observed: Lightning payments can carry more than just sats!
